summary: Root cause identified (confidence 0.80, high): the pricing-engine config flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct was ramped 5→100% at 12:04:00Z, moving essentially all quote traffic onto the CPU-bound GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path (paths=20000), which saturates pricing-engine CPU and blows the 2000ms compute budget; order-service, calling pricing-engine synchronously with a 2500ms timeout, then fails at the quote step. Temporal and causal fit are tight — pricing-engine p99 steps 58.67ms→2528.15ms between 12:03Z and 12:05Z, CPU steps in exactly the 12:04Z bucket matching the config timestamp, and order-service quote timeouts begin 12:06:10Z, ~1 min later — while the compute-bound log signatures name the GreeksV2 calculator and the 2000ms deadline. Competing alternatives are positively contradicted: load growth is excluded by dead-flat request volume, the market-data-service protobuf deploy shows no latency/error discontinuity, and redis-cache health metrics are flat. The one unverified hop is the path-mix shift itself (no per-calculator counter exists), which is why confidence is capped at 0.80 rather than higher.

ranked_hypotheses.title: pricing-engine Greeks v2 flag ramped to 100% saturates CPU and blows the quote compute budget
ranked_hypotheses.statement: At 12:04:00Z the config flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct was ramped 5→100 by pm-experiments, moving essentially all quote traffic onto the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path (paths=20000). That path is CPU-bound; pricing-engine CPU jumps from ~40% baseline to ~99% saturation and per-request compute time rises to multi-second (6465ms, 8361ms observed), blowing the 2000ms budget and pushing p99 from ~60ms to ~2.5s. The CPU step lands exactly in the 12:04Z bucket (40.13%→68.44%, max 98.65), matching the config timestamp, while request volume stayed flat (~625-667 req/s) and upstream demand flat (~230 req/s) — so this is a per-request cost increase, not a volume increase. order-service, calling pricing-engine synchronously with a 2500ms timeout, then times out at the quote step.

causal_chain.claim: Config flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct ramped 5→100 at 12:04:00Z by pm-experiments
Ramp moves ~all quote traffic onto the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo (paths=20000) compute path
pricing-engine CPU steps from ~40% baseline to saturation at exactly the 12:04Z bucket (avg 40.13%→68.44%, max 98.65; ~99-100% from 12:06Z)
Request volume is flat across the onset (pricing-engine ~625-667 req/s; order-service ~230 req/s), so the CPU step is per-request cost, not load
GreeksV2Calculator logs multi-second compute times (6465ms, 8361ms) and 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2'
pricing-engine p99 steps from 58.67ms (12:03Z) to 2528.15ms (12:05Z), persisting ~2550-2750ms
order-service calls pricing-engine synchronously over HTTP with a 2500ms client timeout, so ~2.5s server latency produces client timeouts
order-service error_rate steps to ~8% at the first elevated bucket (12:06Z) and holds

assumptions: The config audit's second shard (which failed to respond in tc-006) does not contain a competing change; tc-014/tc-017 returned partial:false and are treated as complete.
Flag evaluation is effective within ~1 minute of the 12:04Z change entry (no propagation lag beyond the observed step).

The aggregate pricing-engine request_rate being flat means no large volume shift; a per-calculator split is unavailable (F22), so the path-mix shift is inferred from the flag key + GreeksV2 signatures.

ranked_hypotheses.title: pricing-engine capacity saturation from load growth, independent of any change
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine simply ran out of provisioned CPU as quote volume grew toward market open / midday, saturating CPU (~99%) and blowing the compute budget, with the two same-hour changes (flag ramp, protobuf deploy) coincidental. HIST-113 'pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open' is the nearest precedent.

causal_chain.claim: Demand on pricing-engine's quote compute grows beyond provisioned CPU
CPU saturates ~99% and per-request compute time inflates to multiple seconds
p99 steps 58.67ms → 2528.15ms and order-service quote calls time out at 2500ms

assumptions: Quote volume (not path mix) grew enough at 12:04Z to saturate CPU.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Directly contradicted by measured volume: pricing-engine request_rate is dead flat across 11:50-12:15Z (590.66-687.48 req/s, 12:02Z=667.24, 12:04Z=625.14, 12:06Z=666.82) and upstream order-service demand is flat (216.83-242.82 req/s) while CPU goes 40%→99% — so no load growth occurred at onset (F19, F23, F24). The CPU step also aligns to the 12:04Z bucket, exactly the config-flag timestamp, not to any demand curve (F20, F21). The load-growth hop is now positively excluded, not merely unevidenced; HIST-113 remains only a weak symptom-matched lead.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache / downstream dependency degradation degrades the quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A fault on a shared dependency — most plausibly redis-cache, which both pricing-engine and market-data-service use, or another downstream on the synchronous chain — degrades latency, and the resulting slow quote path causes order-service timeouts. Precedent HIST-107 ('Cold cache storm after redis failover') and HIST-113 point toward cache/compute rather than serialization.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache (shared, owner platform) is on the quote path for both pricing-engine and market-data-service
Shared dependency degrades (failover, eviction storm, or resource contention)
pricing-engine p99 steps to ~2.5s and order-service quote calls time out

assumptions: redis-cache or another shared dependency actually degraded.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Now positively contradicted by redis-cache telemetry rather than absence of evidence: evictions_per_min flat (~2-4, 12:02Z=3.11 vs 11:50Z=3.18), connected_clients flat (mean 311.89), hit_ratio_pct flat (mean 96.05%), cpu_pct flat (~22%) across the whole window with no step at 12:03-12:05Z (F27, F28). market-data-service latency and error-rate are also flat (F25, F26), so neither shared-path service shows a regression. Mechanism also fails: pricing-engine's error signatures are explicitly CPU/compute-bound on GreeksV2 with no connection, pool, cache or timeout errors (F2), and CPU saturates in lockstep with p99 while memory stays flat (F5) — local compute, not a remote/cache stall. Note redis-cache exposes no latency metric, so cache-side latency remains unmeasured, but every available health metric is flat.

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf serialization change degrades the quote path (reporter's suspicion)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: market-data-service v5.2.0 switched quote serialization to protobuf at 11:56:00Z. If order-service or pricing-engine cannot correctly/efficiently consume the new format, the synchronous quote path degrades and order-service quote calls time out. On this reading the 12:04Z Greeks v2 ramp is coincidental.

causal_chain.claim: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' deployed 11:56:00Z
New wire format reaches order-service/pricing-engine over the synchronous order-service → pricing-engine → market-data-service HTTP chain
Deserialization/compatibility cost or failure inflates quote-path latency
order-service quote calls exceed 2500ms and error out

assumptions: A protobuf-format regression would manifest as CPU-bound Monte-Carlo compute time (it would not).
Any resulting errors would be absent from logs (they are not — the errors are explicit compute-budget deadlines).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: No supporting mechanism in evidence and now positively contradicted by telemetry: order-service logs contain zero serialization/deserialization errors — every error is 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' (F1); pricing-engine's signature is compute-bound with no serialization/connection errors (F2); market-data-service emits zero WARN/ERROR in 12:00-13:59Z (F6) and, critically, its p99 latency is completely flat across 11:50-13:59Z (mean 39.91ms) with values straddling the 11:56Z deploy within normal variance (11:50Z=40.86, 11:54Z=39.37, 11:58Z=39.06) and its error_rate flat (mean 0.21%) with no step at deploy or at 12:03-12:05Z onset (F25, F26, F29). Timing is also wrong: the deploy precedes the p99 step by ~8 min with no intermediate anomaly, while the flag ramp sits within ~1 min (F16). The flag key names exactly the compute path in the error signatures (F17), and historical precedent search found no serialization-change analogue (F12).

facts.statement: pricing-engine config flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct was ramped 5→100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z by pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'); this is one of only two config changes in 10:00-13:00Z, the other being api-gateway ratelimit.burst 200→250 at 10:30Z.

A second, distinct change landed 8 minutes earlier: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' deployed 2026-05-20T11:56:00Z by v.rao, status live, never rolled back — the only deployment anywhere in the incident window.

pricing-engine request_rate is dead flat across 11:50-12:15Z (590.66-687.48 req/s; 12:02Z=667.24, 12:04Z=625.14, 12:06Z=666.82), and upstream order-service demand is flat (216.83-242.82 req/s; 12:04Z=230.26, 12:06Z=234.78); combined with the CPU step this indicates a per-request cost increase, not a volume increase.

market-data-service p99 latency is flat across 11:50-13:59Z (mean 39.91ms, min 35.28, max 43.75; deploy-straddling buckets 11:50Z=40.86, 11:54Z=39.37, 11:58Z=39.06; onset buckets 12:02Z=39.84, 12:06Z=39.43) with no step at either the 11:56Z deploy or the 12:03-12:05Z onset.

market-data-service error_rate is flat and low across 11:50-13:59Z (mean 0.21%, min 0.1%, max 0.32%); post-deploy 11:58Z=0.22% and onset buckets 12:02Z/12:06Z=0.16%/0.21% — no error-rate step at deploy or onset.
market-data-service emits zero WARN/ERROR in 12:00-13:59Z (total_matched=0), so the reported serialization change leaves no error signature in its logs.

redis-cache metrics are flat through the window: evictions_per_min mean 2.99 (12:02Z=3.11, 12:06Z=3.27 vs 11:50Z=3.18), connected_clients mean 311.89 (12:02Z=316.34, 12:06Z=309.61), hit_ratio_pct mean 96.05% (12:02Z=96.36, 12:06Z=96.73), cpu_pct mean 21.98% (12:02Z=21.98, 12:06Z=22.41) — no step aligned with the 12:03-12:05Z onset.

The quote path is synchronous HTTP end-to-end: order-service → pricing-engine (kind http) → market-data-service (http), with pricing-engine also depending on shared redis-cache; order-service additionally calls exchange-gateway, produces to kafka and uses ledger-db. Both same-hour changes sit on this single chain.
The pre-incident baseline 08:00-11:15Z contains no change other than the api-gateway burst bump at 10:30Z, so nothing landed before 11:56Z to seed a slow-burn onset.

No per-path/per-calculator request counter exists for pricing-engine ('requests_by_calculator' = not_found; available metrics are cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts), so the GreeksV2-vs-other traffic split cannot be measured directly.

Historical precedent search found no serialization-change analogue; nearest symptom matches are HIST-113 (pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open) and HIST-107 (cold cache storm after redis failover).

timeline.event: api-gateway ratelimit.burst raised 200→250 by config-bot; precedes onset by ~94 min and is off the pricing path.
Baseline established: pricing-engine request_rate and order-service demand flat; pricing-engine p99 ~59-61ms and CPU ~40%; redis-cache health metrics flat.
market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' deployed by v.rao (status live, never rolled back) — the only deployment in the window.
Buckets straddling the protobuf deploy show no discontinuity: market-data-service p99 39.06ms and error_rate 0.22%, within normal variance of pre-deploy values.
Still pre-onset: pricing-engine CPU avg 40.13%/max 40.18% and p99 58.67ms-class baseline; request_rate 667.24 req/s and order-service demand 230-235 req/s, all flat.
Last pre-onset bucket: pricing-engine p99 avg 58.67ms.

pricing-engine config flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct ramped 5→100 by pm-experiments, moving ~all quote traffic onto the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path; pricing-engine CPU steps to avg 68.44%/max 98.65 in exactly this bucket, while request volume stays flat.
pricing-engine p99 steps to 2528.15ms (max 2534.9), ~1 min before the first order-service timeout; first compute-bound WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms'.
order-service error_rate steps 0.22%→8.1%; pricing-engine CPU ~99% from here onward; market-data-service p99 (39.43ms) and error_rate (0.21%) remain flat.

First pricing-engine ERROR 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2'.

Symptoms persist to end of data: pricing-engine p99 ~2550-2750ms, order-service ~8% error rate, 225 timeout errors cumulative; redis-cache and market-data-service metrics remain flat.

recommended_actions.action: Roll back the configuration change: revert pricing-engine flag flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 100 back to 5 (config entry made by pm-experiments at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z).
recommended_actions.rationale: The flag ramp 5→100 at 12:04:00Z is the change that moved all traffic onto the CPU-bound GreeksV2 path; the CPU step and p99 step land in exactly the 12:04Z/12:05Z buckets (F8, F13, F20, F21, F3) and order-service timeouts follow ~1 min later (F1). Reverting restores the pre-change path mix.

recommended_actions.action: Hold the market-data-service v5.2.0 protobuf rollout (no further rollout steps) and do NOT roll it back as the primary mitigation, since it is metric-clean.
recommended_actions.rationale: The 11:56Z deploy precedes onset by ~8 min with no intermediate anomaly (F7, F16) and shows flat p99 (39-44ms) and error_rate (0.1-0.32%) across both the deploy and the onset (F25, F26, F29), so rolling it back would be an unmotivated change during an active incident.

recommended_actions.action: Verify recovery after the flag revert within one 120s bucket: confirm pricing-engine CPU returns toward ~40%, p99 returns to ~60ms, order-service error_rate returns toward ~0.2%, and quote timeouts stop.
recommended_actions.rationale: A revert-and-recover confirmation converts the inference-level causal link (no per-calculator counter exists, F22) into a direct measurement and rules out a residual independent fault.

recommended_actions.action: If CPU/p99 do not recover after the revert, re-run the config change audit to cover the failed shard 2/3 and check pricing-engine GC and connection/pool metrics before further mitigation.
recommended_actions.rationale: The config audit retry returned partial:false with count 2, but the first call's shard 2/3 failure (tc-006) leaves a completeness gap, and GC/pool metrics were never queried — both could explain a non-recovering CPU-bound signature.

recommended_actions.action: Right-size the GreeksV2 path before any further ramp: benchmark the Monte-Carlo paths=20000 cost against CPU headroom, and gate the rollout_pct ramp on measured per-request latency versus the 2000ms budget.
recommended_actions.rationale: The observed per-request compute times (6465ms, 8361ms) exceed the 2000ms budget and saturate CPU (F2, F5, F20); the path is CPU-bound and cannot be run at 100% traffic on current capacity.

recommended_actions.action: Add a per-path/per-calculator request and latency counter for pricing-engine (e.g. a GreeksV2-labeled counter) so that path-mix shifts are directly measurable.
recommended_actions.rationale: No such counter exists (requests_by_calculator = not_found), which is the single reason the H1 conclusion rests on inference rather than direct measurement (F22).

recommended_actions.action: Require rollout-percentage changes on CPU-bound code paths to be staged (e.g. 5→25→50→100) with automatic guardrails on p99 latency and CPU saturation that halt or auto-revert the ramp.
recommended_actions.rationale: A single 5→100 step at 12:04Z saturated pricing-engine CPU and took down the order quote path within ~2 minutes; staging plus guardrails would have stopped the ramp at the first elevated bucket (F8, F20, F21).

recommended_actions.action: Add explicit compute-budget/CPU-saturation alerting on pricing-engine with a p99 threshold well below the 2500ms order-service timeout, so saturation pages before order quotes fail.
recommended_actions.rationale: pricing-engine p99 crossed 2528ms ~1 min before the first order-service timeout at 12:06:10Z (F3, F1); alerting on the earlier signal shortens time to detection.

data_gaps: No per-path/per-calculator request counter exists for pricing-engine (requests_by_calculator = not_found; only 6 aggregate metrics), so the GreeksV2-vs-other traffic split at 12:04Z cannot be measured directly — the H1 path-mix hop is inferred from the flag key, the compute-bound signatures and flat aggregate volume.

market-data-service metric queries were never run (logs only, zero WARN/ERROR; request_rate/cpu_pct queries hit budget_exhausted), so a silent, log-free metric regression in that service cannot be fully excluded — though p99 and error_rate were later confirmed flat.

redis-cache exposes no latency or p95/p99 metric (available: connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct), so cache-side latency — the metric most directly on the quote path — is unmeasured; health is judged indirectly via hit ratio, evictions, connections and CPU.
pricing-engine GC metrics and connection/pool metrics were not queried, so whether GC pauses contribute to the p99 rise is unchecked.

The first config-change audit returned partial:true (shard 2/3 did not respond); the retry returned partial:false with count 2, but a third shard's completeness could not be independently verified, so an additional competing config change cannot be fully ruled out.
No revert or rollback record exists in-window for either the 12:04Z flag ramp or the 11:56Z deploy, so the change history alone cannot confirm that reverting the flag stops the incident.

No historical precedent for a protobuf/serialization-change-induced latency regression was found (the second historical search was not executed); nearest analogues are capacity_saturation (HIST-113) and cache/infra failure (HIST-107).

order-service and pricing-engine error_rate/CPU metrics are 240s-bucketed, so the exact minute of order-service error_rate onset cannot be pinned below ~12:02-12:06Z granularity; only the 120s p99 series resolves pricing-engine onset to ~1 min.
No api-gateway ingress request-count metric was checked; order-service request_rate was used as the tighter upstream-demand proxy.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Reverting flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct to 5 without recovery of pricing-engine CPU (~40%) and p99 (~60ms) — that would mean the GreeksV2 path mix is not the cause and the flag timing was coincidental.
Evidence of a per-path request counter showing pricing-engine traffic did NOT shift onto GreeksV2 at 12:04Z (currently unmeasurable, F22), which would remove H1's mechanism.
A latency/error discontinuity in market-data-service metrics (p99 or 5xx) at the 11:56Z deploy or the 12:03-12:05Z onset, contradicting the flat p99/error_rate readings (F25, F26, F29).

A redis-cache latency measurement (currently unavailable) showing a step at 12:03-12:05Z, which would resurrect a shared-dependency explanation despite flat hit ratio/evictions/clients/CPU (F27, F28).
Discovery of an additional config change on the unverified audit shard 2/3 with a timestamp inside the 12:03-12:05Z onset window, which would create a competing origin.

Evidence that pricing-engine request volume or upstream order-service demand actually surged at 12:04Z (e.g. 120s-resolution data refuting the flat 590-687 req/s and 217-243 req/s readings), which would re-open H4 load growth.
Evidence tying the compute overspend to GC pauses or connection/pool exhaustion rather than the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path, which would change the mechanism within the pricing-engine origin.
Proof that the market-data-service protobuf format is consumed inefficiently by order-service/pricing-engine at a level invisible to current logs and metrics, which would revive H2.
